passages.t: Joshua in filthy clothes, and the accuser rebuked
passages.happening:
The angel shows Zechariah ‘Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, with Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him’ (verse 1). The LORD rebukes the accuser: the LORD, who has chosen Jerusalem, rebukes him, and Joshua is ‘a firebrand snatched from the fire’ (verse 2).

Joshua stands in filthy clothes (verse 3). The angel orders them taken off and tells Joshua that his iniquity has been removed and he will be clothed in splendid robes (verse 4). Zechariah asks that a clean turban be put on his head, and it is done, with the angel of the LORD standing by (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Joshua son of Jehozadak was the first high priest after the exile. His father had been carried into exile, and his grandfather Seraiah, chief priest when Jerusalem fell, was executed by Nebuchadnezzar. Joshua had come back with Zerubbabel and led in rebuilding the altar. As the temple rose, the question of his fitness would have been pressing: a priest who grew up in an unclean foreign land, representing a people whose sin had brought the exile.

The scene is a heavenly law court. An accuser stood at the right hand of the accused. The Hebrew has the satan, with the article, meaning the accuser or adversary, a figure who appears in a similar role in the heavenly court in Job. Whether the word is a name or a title is debated, but the role is clear: he brings charges.

The clothes matter because of the priestly law. The high priest wore garments made for glory and beauty, and a turban bearing a gold plate engraved Holy to the LORD. Filthy clothes would make him unfit. God answers the accusation not by denying the guilt but by removing it.
passages.later: The accuser stands in the heavenly court in Job (Job 1:6). The high priest's turban carried a gold plate inscribed ‘HOLY TO THE LORD’ (Exodus 28:36).
passages.asks: The accuser was right about Joshua's filthy clothes, and God removed them anyway. Ask what accusation you keep hearing against yourself. And ask what it would mean to let God clothe you instead.

passages.happening:
The angel of the LORD gives Joshua a charge. If he walks in God's ways and keeps his instructions, he will govern God's house and have charge of his courts, and have a place among those standing there (verses 6-7).

‘Hear now, O high priest Joshua, you and your companions seated before you, who are indeed a sign. For behold, I am going to bring My servant, the Branch’ (verse 8). Before Joshua is a stone with seven eyes, on which God will engrave an inscription, and he will remove the iniquity of the land in a single day (verse 9). On that day everyone will invite a neighbor to sit under vine and fig tree (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Joshua and his fellow priests are a sign, a living pointer to something God will do. The Branch is a title from Jeremiah for a king from David's line, a shoot growing from a stump that seemed dead. In chapter 6 the Branch will build the temple.

The vine and fig tree were a picture of peace and plenty, every family on its own land with no one to frighten it, as in the days of Solomon and in Micah's promise.

To remove the land's guilt in a single day recalls the Day of Atonement, when the high priest made atonement for the whole people once a year.
passages.later: Jeremiah promised, ‘I will raise up for David a righteous Branch’ (Jeremiah 23:5). Micah pictured each person under his own vine and fig tree (Micah 4:4).
passages.hard:
What is the stone with seven eyes in verse 9?

This is one of the book's puzzles, and interpreters disagree. Some take the stone as a precious stone for the high priest's clothing, perhaps the gold plate on the turban, which was engraved with an inscription; the verb for engrave is the same one used there. Others take it as a building stone for the temple, perhaps the capstone or foundation stone connected with Zerubbabel in 4:7-10. The seven eyes may be read as facets, as springs, since the Hebrew word for eye can also mean spring, or as the eyes of the LORD that range over the whole earth, as in 4:10. These notes do not settle it. The verse's own point is clear: God will remove the land's guilt in one day.
passages.asks: God promises to remove the guilt of the land in a single day. Ask what guilt you have carried long after God offered to take it. And ask what it would look like to invite your neighbor under your vine and fig tree.
